Iren is the same trade with a darker-pool tell. It printed about $727 million of dark-pool volume the same day it delivered Horizon 1 to Microsoft, the biggest single-day dark print in a year, and it has 85 percent of year-end capacity contracted toward a $4.4 billion ARR target. The spot market backs the thesis: a three-year-old A100 generation is contracted through 2029 at full freight, and Nebius's first capacity auction cleared 15 percent above the prior record. CME plans to list compute futures in October, with Larry Fink calling compute a financialized resource, the market formalizing the scarcity the neoclouds are selling.

3. The optics stack is the quietest part of the AI trade and the one compounding fastest. The photonics names are printing the kind of numbers memory did two months ago. Applied Optoelectronics is the top pick, with its data-center revenue up from $32 million to $81.4 million year over year, a first 1.6T order above $200 million, and a $1 billion 2026 revenue target that would be up 107.6 percent. Lumentum did Q3 revenue of $808.4 million, up 90 percent, and guided Q4 to $960 million to $1.01 billion. Marvell's Q1 was a record $2.418 billion, up 28 percent, with Celestial AI capacity set to double by fiscal 2028. Coherent carries a $2 billion Nvidia equity stake on top of the optics cycle.

These four names have a common thread: they are the physical layer the hyperscalers cannot buy fast enough, and unlike the memory names they have not had their squeeze already. When Nvidia confirms the buildout on August 26, the optics complex is the group that has not yet repriced for it.

4. The fintech and consumer corners still work on their own numbers. Nu Holdings put up its first billion-dollar quarter, net income of $1.06 billion, up 67 percent, on revenue up 39 percent with return on equity at 33 percent, and the stock rose about 10 percent. The credit tell is the same one the house flagged in the Macro edition last week: 90-day nonperforming loans ticked up to 6.9 percent from 6.5 percent, the highest since 2024, on a portfolio up 37 percent. Nu is a real growth lender, but it is also the first place Latin consumer stress shows up.

Jack in the Box is the contrarian value setup. It trades at about 0.22 times sales against Papa John's at 0.5, Wendy's at 0.6, Starbucks at 3 and McDonald's at 7, after falling from $100 to about $10 and now consolidating. The bull case is that the discount already prices the decline and the franchise is stable enough to re-rate. The bear case is that a broken consumer hurts a value burger chain first. Either way the asymmetry is unusual for a name this beaten down.

5. The froth is real, and it is the counterweight to every bull case this week. Margin debt sits at a record near $1.5 trillion, up 49 percent year over year, about 4 percent of GDP against a 50-year norm near 1.5 percent, and the Shiller CAPE is near 41 against a long-run median of 16. About half of retail options volume is now same-day expiries. Roughly $3 trillion of AI data centers is financed with borrowed money and the industry needs close to $1.5 trillion more by 2028. South Korea is the cautionary example: the KOSPI doubled, retail poured in $70 billion net, and July was a 22 percent drawdown, the worst since the global financial crisis.

None of this makes the bull case wrong. It makes it fragile, and the fragility lives in the leverage, not in the earnings. Into a record close on thin volume with a leveraged book, the position to hold is the one that does not need the market to be right every day.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU. Back above the 50-day for the first time in weeks, with resistance at 1022, 1064, 1082, 1121 and 1155, and BofA's $236 fiscal-2030 EPS model points at a four-figure price. Apple-off-China-memory is a fresh tailwind into Nvidia earnings.
  • $NBIS. Q2 revenue up 454 percent, a 41 percent EBITDA margin, and a backlog above $40 billion, with Koss guiding 2027 ARR past $20 billion. The $277 price is the discount to that.
  • $IREN. The $727 million dark-pool day and 85 percent of year-end capacity contracted toward a $4.4 billion ARR target. The neocloud path to $200 runs through Microsoft and the 2027 buildout.
  • $NU. First quarter above a billion dollars of net income, ROE at 33 percent, stock up 10 percent. The 6.9 percent NPL tick is the tell that decides whether this re-rates or rolls over.
  • $JACK. 0.22 times sales against a market that pays 3 to 7 times for peers, after a 90 percent drawdown that is now consolidating. A broken-valuation setup with a live bear case.

item.title: SanDisk's investor day put a floor under the memory trade, and Micron ran at $1,000
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: SanDisk guided to roughly 80 percent gross margins through 2030 on $94 billion of locked contracts, JPMorgan set a $2,250 target, and Micron cleared $965 on its way at the four-figure line.
item.content:encoded:
SanDisk guided to roughly 80 percent gross margins through 2030 on $94 billion of locked contracts, JPMorgan set a $2,250 target, and Micron cleared $965 on its way at the four-figure line.

Yesterday the question was whether Nebius could hold its run against Burry. Today the memory complex answered a bigger one, and the S&P closed at another record on top of it.

Market context. The S&P 500 closed at a record 7,798.99 after clearing 7,800 intraday, with the Nasdaq up 0.81 percent. Hedge funds bought $6.8 billion of US equities last week, the largest weekly buy in 18 years, while retail sold $4.1 billion and institutions sold $1.1 billion. The tape rotated into semis and neoclouds. Options volume leaders were Nvidia at 2.4 million contracts, Tesla at 2.0 million, and Micron at 1.0 million, with Nvidia earnings now eight trading days out on August 26.

The scoreboard. I said on July 30 that the July low holds into mid-August, and I trimmed the odds to 60/40 the week after. The S&P is now at an all-time high with hedge funds re-grossing at an 18-year pace, so that low held and then some. Hit.

1. SanDisk put a number on the memory supercycle and Micron ran at $1,000. SanDisk's investor day was not a story, it was a guide. The company is targeting roughly 80 percent non-GAAP gross margins through fiscal 2030 on about $94 billion of locked long-term contracts, with multi-year agreements already covering half of fiscal 2027 bit supply and two-thirds by 2028. JPMorgan resumed coverage at overweight with a $2,250 target and a view that the contracts hold margins even at floor pricing. The stock closed up about 14 percent Thursday and added roughly 6 percent premarket, and it is up about 50 percent since the fund that blew up on it liquidated.

Micron is doing the tape's work on the way to four figures. It hit $987 premarket, cleared the $965 target the house has been tracking, and needs a close above $991 to confirm the next leg toward $1,022. The structural numbers underneath are the ones that matter: about 70 percent of hyperscaler capex is now going to memory, the projected 2027 spend is $761 billion, demand is growing roughly 200 percent a year against 20 percent supply, and UBS models DRAM undersupplied until the second quarter of 2028. SK Hynix's chairman said the shortage worsens into 2027 and that even doubling capacity in five years is not enough.

The skeptical read is real and it came from the desks today, with some calling SanDisk's HBF marketing and dividing the addressable market by two to four. That is the debate the whole memory thesis turns on, and it is live, not settled.

2. The neoclouds got validation, and the rentals are pricing it. Iren delivered Horizon 1 to Microsoft, earning Nvidia's Exemplar Cloud status, and guided to about $3.4 billion of annualized AI Cloud revenue by the end of 2026 on the $9.7 billion Microsoft deal, with capacity moving from 480 megawatts to 1.2 gigawatts through 2027. CoreWeave's CEO said the company signed $25 billion-plus of new contracts in the five weeks since its quarter closed and that the depreciation debate is put to bed, pointing to Blackwell B200 rental rates that have climbed from roughly $2 per GPU hour a year ago to just under $4 now. Nebius held the Northland Street-high buy at a $410 target on $582 million of revenue up 454 percent.

The common thread is pricing power in the spot market. When a three-year-old GPU generation is contracted out to 2029 at full freight, the supply is not loose, and the neoclouds are being paid for it.

3. Nu Holdings put up its first billion-dollar quarter. Nu did $1.06 billion of net income in the quarter, up 67 percent and the first quarter above a billion, on revenue of $5.88 billion, up 39 percent, with return on equity at 33 percent and net interest margin at 22.9 percent. The stock rose about 10 percent. The number to watch is the credit one: 90-day nonperforming loans ticked up to 6.9 percent from 6.5, the highest since the third quarter of 2024, on a portfolio up 37 percent to $39.4 billion. That is the first sign of the consumer stress the Macro edition flagged, showing up in a Brazilian lender before it reaches US names.

4. ZIM is a cash machine that trades like a shipping line. The container carrier trades near $27.50 with roughly $25 a share of cash on the balance sheet, so the market is paying about two and a half dollars for the shipping franchise. Second-quarter cash generation is on track to add $8 to $10 a share by the third quarter, and the desks put assets plus cash near $100 a share against an $8 to $14 earnings range. That is a broken-valuation setup in a name the market is treating as cyclical at the bottom.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SNDK. Investor day guided to roughly 80 percent gross margins through 2030 on $94 billion of contracts, JPMorgan set a $2,250 target, and the stock is up about 50 percent since the forced liquidation. The marketing-versus-real debate is live.
  • $MU. At $987 and through the $965 target, with $991 the confirmation line toward $1,022. Memory at 70 percent of hyperscaler capex and DRAM undersupplied to Q2 2028 is the structural case.
  • $NBIS. Northland's Street-high $410 target on $582 million of revenue up 454 percent and the ability to sell 2027 capacity today. Burry is still short from higher.
  • $NU. First quarter above $1 billion of net income, ROE at 33 percent, stock up 10 percent. The 6.9 percent NPL tick is the credit tell to watch into next quarter.
  • $ZIM. About $25 a share of cash against a $27.50 price, assets plus cash near $100. The market is pricing the shipping line as cyclical at the bottom while the cash stack grows.

item.title: Nebius ran 34 percent, Burry doubled down, and the S&P broke 7,800
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Nebius posted 454 percent revenue growth on $582 million, raised its contract book to $46 billion, and the afternoon brought Burry with a fresh short at $247 plus a $94 billion memory thesis that nobody was carrying this morning.
item.content:encoded:
Nebius posted 454 percent revenue growth on $582 million, raised its contract book to $46 billion, and the afternoon brought Burry with a fresh short at $247 plus a $94 billion memory thesis that nobody was carrying this morning.

Yesterday I said the neocloud earnings were the real news and the depreciation argument had no purchase on a business that pre-sells capacity above cost. Today the market agreed and kept going.

Market context. Per the Market morning list, the S&P 500 broke above 7,800 for the first time ever in a session that opened green on the post-CPI momentum and kept running. The VIX touched 14.39, its lowest level of the year, on the lightest volume in thirteen sessions. The S&P has now printed 26 all-time highs this year. $NVDA closed at $224, its first close above 220 in a month. $META fell 3.3 percent and $MSFT 2.2, the rotation inside the rally that says semis are back and the software trade is taking a breather. Options volume leaders: NVDA 3.6 million contracts, SMCI 720,000, MU 1.3 million.

1. Nebius put up the numbers and Burry answered with a bigger short. Per the Crypto PM list and the Stocks PM list, Nebius did $582.3 million of revenue against $573 million expected, up 454 percent year over year. Adjusted EBITDA was $236 million against $173 million. AI Cloud revenue rose 514 percent. The company raised contracted capacity to 5 gigawatts, expects more than 1 gigawatt a year of deployment from 2027, and carried about $46 billion of multi-year AI cloud contracts including $27 billion with $META and $17 billion with $MSFT. Customer prepayments are expected to top $9 billion in 2026 alone, at 50 to 60 percent of capex.

Per the Stocks PM list, the pricing is the real weapon. Nebius signed its first deal at $40 to $50 million per megawatt, against a normal rate of about $20 to $25 million and a baseline of $9.8 million. Its first capacity auction cleared 15 percent above the highest price it had ever charged for Blackwell. It could sell its entire 2027 capacity today and is choosing not to. Per Shay Boloor, short-notice deals pay back in under two years with customers funding roughly half the capex upfront.

The stock ran from roughly $195 to $275 before fading slightly in the close, a move that puts Burry's $211.77 short from Tuesday underwater and his new $247 short from today barely flat. Per burrytracker, Burry added NBIS shorts at $247, MU short at $924, and ORCL short at $152 today, with a quote that Nebius is what the top of a boom looks like. Per the Jose Najarro stream, the question is how many of his 300,000 Substack followers are covering a 30 percent short float in a stock that is up ten times in eighteen months and answering on every quarter.

The after-hours earnings gave the longs a breather. NBIS faded about half a percent in sympathy with Cerebras, which fell 14 percent on operating expense of $500 million against $80 million expected at a $60 billion market cap. At that valuation on less than a billion of revenue, the credibility was inside the margin math.

2. SanDisk just put a match to the memory complex, and the size of the thesis is what matters. Per the Market PM list, SanDisk unveiled its HBF architecture, NAND repurposed as AI memory, and the numbers are not incremental. HBF matches high-bandwidth memory at 12.8 terabytes per second of bandwidth while using one-eighth the GPU resources at one-quarter the footprint. It achieves twice the GPU efficiency at one-eighth the capex, because one HBF GPU runs the same model that requires eight HBM GPUs.

Per Shay Boloor, SanDisk guided mid-to-high-teens revenue growth, roughly 80 percent non-GAAP gross margins, and about 50 percent adjusted free cash flow margins, with 100 percent of excess cash returned. Eight customers have signed contracts totalling roughly $94 billion in lifetime value. Key-value cache workloads are expected to drive 35 percent of AI data centre NAND workloads by 2030, and BiCS NAND delivers 54 percent more bits per wafer at 27 percent annual productivity improvement. Sell-side targets are running back to $3,000 from the current $1,404.

This is a thesis that would exist even if Nvidia stayed flat. The memory call the house has been fighting over for two weeks is now sitting on top of a named architecture with numbers, and the argument over whether multiples expand or compress just got a third term that neither side was pricing.

3. AMAT reported a beat and fell on it, and the month has a new earnings rhythm. Per the Reddit post and the Stocks AM list, Applied Materials beat earnings and raised guidance on its semiconductor systems, guided AGS revenue growth above 20 percent and advanced-packaging revenue growth above 70 percent for 2026, and fell 5 percent after hours because the expectations were higher than the beat. That is the same pattern Cerebras hit and the same one Coherent hit with a double beat that faded six percent: the bar for a clean after-hours reaction on earnings day inside a stock at an all-time high is not a beat, it is a blowout, and nothing short of a blowout that clears the valuation question gets a pass.

Per the Chip Stock Investor stream, DigitalOcean raised full-year guidance to 30 to 31 percent from 25 to 27, called for 50 percent growth by the end of fiscal 2027 on $400 million a quarter, and an analyst noted the cleanest balance sheet in the cloud infrastructure space with net cash and stock buybacks actively offsetting dilution. The stock faded after its own Q2 but the guidance keeps stacking.

Per the Financial Markets AM list, Coherent did $2.1 billion against $1.98 billion, guided Q1 to $2.3 billion against $2.1 billion, and has its revenue trajectory pointing above $3 billion a quarter by the end of fiscal 2027 on a backlog booked through calendar 2027. The after-hours faded anyway.

The Meta and Microsoft drops inside an index making all-time highs are the same signal in reverse. $META down 3.3 and $MSFT down 2.2 tells you this is a rotation within the rally, not a distribution event. The semis ran, the software gave back, Cisco beat on networking up 40 percent and faded in sympathy, and the after-hours trade painted its own picture.

4. Ackman rebuilt his portfolio and Peltz is coming for Wendy's. Per the Market AM list and Walter Bloomberg, Bill Ackman added six new holdings in his biggest portfolio revamp in years: $NFLX, $V, $MA, $ALC, $ICE and $SPGI. He bought $NFLX in 2022 at about $350 a share for $1.1 billion, sold at a roughly $400 million loss, and is now back in with the stock roughly half what he paid. His thesis is double-digit revenue compounding and about 20 percent annual earnings growth. Pershing Square USA is down 3.5 percent through July against the S&P up 13.

Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management is preparing a take-private of Wendy's at up to $8.80 a share with a consortium including BlueFive Capital and the Flynn Group. The stock has a 30 percent short float on 160 million shares and Heisenberg called the price today directly.

Per the Reddit post and Bloomberg, the California Public Utilities Commission was scheduled to vote today on Charter Communications' merger with Cox, the last major regulatory step before it becomes the largest broadband and cable provider in the United States at 38 million subscribers surpassing Comcast. The stock trades at $150 on a 3.9 times earnings multiple with $4.9 billion of net income and a 50 percent short float, and the SpaceX consumer mobile partnership talks reported by Bloomberg and Reuters in June sit on the other side of the close.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $NBIS. $582 million of revenue, 454 percent growth, $46 billion in contracts, and the ability to charge $50 million a megawatt on short notice against a baseline of $10 million. Burry is short at $247 and the stock touched $275 same day.
  • $SNDK. $94 billion of lifetime contracts on a memory architecture that matches HBM bandwidth at one-eighth the capex. The re-rate is priced at $1,404 and the sellers are calling $3,000.
  • $MU. At $890 with a 50-day moving average at 965 and the memory complex catching the SNDK halo. The buyback and dividend lift around December 6 is the first hard catalyst this name has had in months.
  • $DOCN. Guidance raised to 30 to 31 percent growth with 50 percent by end of fiscal 2027, a clean balance sheet, active buybacks, and a customer pipeline that is scaling faster than the capacity.
  • $CHTR. CPUC voted today on the Cox merger. At $150 on a 3.9 times multiple with a 50 percent short float and a SpaceX partnership rumor sitting on the other side of the close.

item.title: Both neoclouds beat, Burry got squeezed, and my memory reversal was wrong
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Nebius put up 454 percent revenue growth and CoreWeave broke a five-quarter losing streak on earnings day, while Goldman modelled DRAM prices up 250 to 300 percent next year.
item.content:encoded:
Nebius put up 454 percent revenue growth and CoreWeave broke a five-quarter losing streak on earnings day, while Goldman modelled DRAM prices up 250 to 300 percent next year.

Two days ago I reversed the memory call to compression on the argument that five-year contracts had capped the pricing lever. Today Goldman published a DRAM price forecast that makes that look like the wrong read of the wrong market.

Market context. Per the Kalshi morning list, Tuesday closed with the S&P down 0.3 percent, the Nasdaq 100 down 0.6 and the Russell 2000 up 0.3. Today opened green on the in-line CPI Macro has, then chopped on the lightest volume in thirteen sessions, with Fear and Greed at 62. The drawdowns underneath the index are the part to hold onto: per the Financial Markets list, from all-time highs $META is off 27 percent, $GOOGL 16.4, $AAPL 13 and $MSFT 10.8, with $NVDA down only 5.5.

The scoreboard.

  • Hit. My CoreWeave call said the print turns on whether the first quarter was the true bottom in adjusted operating margin. It was. Section one.
  • Miss. My Nebius call carried Rick Orford's bearish framing at 105.5 times sales with Burry short at $211.77. Nebius beat and ran more than 20 percent. Section one.
  • Miss. My Supermicro call carried Rick Orford's bearish case from July 28. Revenue came in at $11.1 billion against $11.55 billion expected, adjusted earnings at $1.70 against $0.96, and the stock rose 8 to 10 percent after hours because the guide was the story: next quarter $14.5 to $15.5 billion against $11.68 billion, and full-year 2027 $65 to $72 billion against a $52.5 billion consensus. The bear case was right on the facts and a backlog guide beat a balance sheet.
  • Reversing again, and this one needs an explanation rather than a number. The memory call goes back to 60/40 that multiples expand before they compress. Section two is why, and why I should not have moved it on Monday.
  • Confirmed, and my number was light. My July 22 call said Paramount owes a ticking fee above $600 million a quarter if the deal does not close by September 30. It is $7 million a day from October 1, about $637 million a quarter, with trial set for May 2, 2027 and roughly $1.2 billion accrued by then.

1. Both neoclouds beat, and the pricing disclosure is the real news. Per the Stocks morning list, CoreWeave did $2.6 billion of revenue against $2.56 billion expected, adjusted EBITDA of $1.5 billion against $1.43 billion at a 59 percent margin, with backlog at about $104 billion, up 46 percent, and full-year guidance raised to $12.4 to $13.2 billion. Per the People to follow morning list, earnings came in at minus $1.14 against minus $1.45 expected, a 21 percent beat, on a net loss that widened to $626 million.

Per the Market morning list, it ran from minus 3 percent to plus 14.39 percent within an hour, its first green earnings reaction in six tries after five straight of minus 11.4, minus 18.5, minus 16.3, minus 20.8 and minus 2.5.

Nebius was the bigger number. Per the People to follow list:

Nebius Q2Figure
Revenue$582.3 million against $572.75 million expected, up 454 percent
Adjusted EBITDA$236 million against $173 million expected
Contracted capacity guideraised to 5 gigawatts from over 4
Customer prepayments expected in 2026over $9 billion, at 50 to 60 percent of capex
AI cloud adjusted EBITDA margin24 percent, then 45, now 50 across three quarters

The disclosure that matters is what a megawatt costs. Per the Stocks list, mid-term deals run $20 to $25 million per megawatt with half to sixty percent of the capex paid upfront, short deals run $40 to $50 million, and the first capacity auction cleared 15 percent above the highest price it had ever charged for Blackwell. Management said it could sell all of 2027 today and is choosing not to.

That is the answer to the depreciation argument, and it does not require anyone to win a debate about useful life. Burry's short says these companies overstate profits by depreciating GPUs too slowly. Nebius is being paid more per megawatt each quarter and collecting most of the capex before the machines run. Per Edelbridge Alpha, its $775 million facility at SOFR plus 250 covers more than 100 percent of the capex it funds and is repeatable against more than $40 billion of contracted revenue. A business that pre-sells capacity above cost does not need the accounting to be generous.

The counterweight is what Nvidia's $500 billion actually is. Per TBPN, the mechanism is securitization: Nvidia supplies depreciation insurance up to 25 percent plus reference designs that make data centres fungible, so the debt can be tranched into investment-grade paper and sold to pension funds and insurers. The banks are swapping project-specific credit risk for sector-wide risk and collecting fees for the trip. Per Milk Road AI, the money is "not in 2026 or 2027, but over time," and across six sources today nobody produced a per-firm number or a first-dollar date. Treat it as a distribution channel that has been built, not as demand that has been committed.

2. I generalised a NAND concession to DRAM, and that was the error. On Monday I reversed this call because Chip Stock Investor, holding SanDisk through a drawdown, conceded that five-year hyperscaler agreements had ended the wild average selling prices. That concession was real and it was about NAND.

Per the Stocks morning list, the DRAM market is going the other way and the sell side is not being subtle about it. Goldman revised DRAM price forecasts to up 250 to 300 percent in 2026 and up 300 to 350 percent in 2027. Bernstein models average selling prices reaching $2.23 a gigabyte by the end of 2027, roughly five times the 2025 level. Micron posted an 81.2 percent operating margin.

Per the Stocks list, the mechanism is capacity rather than sentiment. A gigabyte of high-bandwidth memory takes three times the wafer capacity of standard DRAM, so every line converted to HBM removes conventional supply at the same time and you get a shortage in both at once. Operating margins across all three makers run 70 to 80 percent. The confirming detail is small and hard to argue with: Google raised the Pixel 11 by $100 to $899 and cited a severe memory crunch.

So the call goes back to 60/40 that multiples expand first, and I am flagging it as low conviction rather than pretending this is insight. I have moved this three times in seven days. A call that moves three times in a week is one I do not have an edge on, and the honest label is a view rather than a position. What I got wrong was treating one company's NAND contract structure as the whole memory complex.

3. Goldman bought an ETF issuer, and it is the second one this year. Per Eric Balchunas, Goldman Sachs is acquiring Neos ETFs for $2.3 billion. Neos is only a few years old and got big fast, at $32 billion, mostly in covered-call monthly income funds. Goldman bought Innovator, the buffered-ETF house, immediately before it, and Balchunas reads the pair as a bet on what he calls boomer candy.

Two acquisitions in a row in defined-outcome and income products is a house buying what sells when investors stop trusting the index. That is a read on flows rather than markets, from a firm that spent this morning declaring a September hold.

4. Texas just cut its own power forecast in half, the first hard brake on the buildout. Per the Polymarket morning list, Texas cut its 2027 power demand growth forecast to 6 percent from 14 after auditing data centre interconnection requests. Per the Stocks list, ERCOT has paused new power deals to Texas data centres outright.

Set that against what power is fetching. Galaxy leased 800 megawatts to CoreWeave at $1.2 billion a year, and its Helios II block of 830 megawatts is expected to clear above $1.4 billion.

The audit is the interesting half. If the queues were inflated by speculative requests, the demand figure everyone has been underwriting was inflated too, and the constraint moves from generation to permission. Names holding energised capacity get more valuable and names holding a pipeline get less. That is a sorting mechanism rather than a sector call.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $NBIS. Revenue up 454 percent, contracted capacity guided to 5 gigawatts, and megawatt pricing stepping from $12 million to $20 million to above $40 million on short deals. It closed Tuesday at $193 and traded around $225. Burry is short from $211.77 and now underwater.
  • $CRWV. A 59 percent adjusted EBITDA margin, $104 billion of backlog and a first green earnings reaction in six quarters, against a net loss widening to $626 million and over $10 billion of new unsecured debt. The margin question is answered and the funding question is not.
  • $MU. An 81.2 percent operating margin into Goldman modelling DRAM up 250 to 300 percent next year, with HBM conversion shorting conventional supply at the same time. The buyback and dividend restriction lifts around December 6, the first dated catalyst this name has had in months. 891 has to hold and 955 is the line above.
  • $FCX. Per Joseph Hogue and Ross Givens, new copper mines take 15 to 20 years and AI alone could lift demand by half. It trades at 20 times this year against a five-year average of 21 after a 58 percent run, with 30 percent profit growth modelled next year.
  • $GS. Two ETF acquisitions in a row, Innovator and now NEOS at up to $2.3 billion for $32 billion of mostly covered-call assets. The buyer of income and buffer products is telling you what it expects investors to want next.

item.title: The Micron bull case arrived and quietly changed the subject away from price
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Rick Orford's hidden moat turns out to be automotive and robotics lock-in, and he concedes analysts expect margins to normalize once supply catches demand.
item.content:encoded:
Rick Orford's hidden moat turns out to be automotive and robotics lock-in, and he concedes analysts expect margins to normalize once supply catches demand.

Yesterday I reversed the memory call to 55/45 that multiples compress before they expand, on the argument that five-year hyperscaler contracts capped the pricing lever. Today the counter-case showed up, and it never mentions pricing.

Market context. The tape did nothing while it waited. Per the Financial Markets list, the S&P touched a session low down almost 0.2 percent in the afternoon and both it and the Nasdaq proxy sat near the lows of the day, with CPI tomorrow the only thing anyone would name as a reason. Monday finished roughly unchanged near 7,753. The breadth underneath is better than the headline: the equal-weight S&P printed new all-time highs, and J.C. Parets has the average Nasdaq 100 stock as strong as it has ever been. Per the Market list, Heisenberg called the gold fund at $370 and it hit $404 today, and he is trimming half.

The scoreboard.

  • Held, and the counter-case did not touch it. My 55/45 that memory multiples compress first. Section one is why the bull argument moving to automotive strengthens it rather than weakening it.
  • Reported today, result not in hand. Supermicro, on Rick Orford's July 28 bearish case. Not one source across today's material carries a number from it, so it stays open rather than getting graded on a guess.
  • Reports tonight, not Wednesday. CoreWeave, against a June quarter consensus of $2.56 billion on EPS of minus $1.45. I had the date a day late.
  • Reports Wednesday. Nebius, and it walked into the print with a problem. Section three.

1. The Micron bull case changed the subject, and that is the strongest thing I learned today. Per Rick Orford, Micron's hidden moat is automotive and robotics end-market diversification, held together by long-term strategic customer agreements with automakers that give certainty on supply and pricing. The supporting numbers are real: cars with L2-plus autonomy need more than five times the memory of a typical vehicle and are over 20 percent of new sales this year, heading to 40 by 2030, and a humanoid robot needs about ten times an L2 car.

Notice what is absent. He never addresses contract against spot pricing, never mentions the five-year hyperscaler agreements, and never uses the phrase take-or-pay. He also concedes the other side outright, saying the market believes the company is near peak earnings and that analysts expect margins to normalize once supply catches up with demand. His answer is that the floor under each cycle keeps rising, and that is a decade-long argument rather than a next-quarter one.

A bull case that retreats from pricing to end markets is a bull case that has conceded the near term. I am holding 55/45.

The valuation is the honest tension. Micron trades at 9.2 times earnings against SK Hynix at 19, with 40 analysts at strong buy and targets implying 82 to 144 percent upside. Cheap is not the same as early.

The rest of the tape is split. Per the Stocks list, Kyle Reidhead's UBS model has DRAM margins rising to a 95 percent peak by late 2027 with commodity DRAM going $11 to $18 a gigabyte, and calls the cyclical thesis dead until 2029. In the same feed Milk Road's house view is a bust in 18 to 24 months, and intelfabs draws the line that matters: HBM margins hold near 75 percent while conventional DRAM walks a classic commoditization path. That split is where this call settles.

2. A pathologist made the clearest bear case of the day and it is not about AI. Per Chip Stock Investor, Dr. Bradley Gibson's mechanism is that Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement is frozen in nominal dollars while costs inflate. The CMS conversion factor was $31 in 1992 and $32.34 in 2025 against more than 120 percent of cumulative inflation.

The dated catalyst is small and specific. His practice got an email last month about a 4.3 percent across-the-board Medicaid cut in Kentucky because the state ran out of money, and close to a third of Kentucky's roughly 130 hospitals already lose money even after subsidy.

Where the exposure sitsThe number
Healthcare as a share of GDPabout 18 percent, roughly $4 trillion a year
Against total income tax receiptsabout $2 trillion
DaVita's dialysis windowthe 30-month private-to-Medicaid transition pays 3 to 4x Medicaid rates and is responsible for essentially 100 percent of operating profit
UnitedHealthemploys 90,000 doctors, just under 10 percent of US physicians, and swung from +$7 billion to a roughly $1 billion loss in 2025

His rule is to bucket by who actually pays: avoid reimbursement-dependent providers and insurers, prefer pharma and especially medical hardware and software that price in cash and sell internationally. He is bearish on AI drug discovery too, because AI speeds discovery while the trials hold the cost.

3. Rocket Lab and AST both reported, both moved, and both finished flat. Per the People to follow list, Rocket Lab did $234 million of revenue against $231 million expected, up 62 percent, with backlog at $2.36 billion, up 137 percent, and guided the third quarter to $250 to $265 million against a $239 million estimate. It missed on EPS at minus $0.08 and guided an adjusted EBITDA loss of $17 to $23 million against $11.8 million expected.

AST SpaceMobile was the messier one: revenue $32 million against $34 million, EPS of minus $0.77 against minus $0.29, more than a two-times miss, with 2026 revenue guidance nonetheless raised to $175 million.

The reaction is the lesson. Heisenberg had the expected move on both above 11 percent, and by half an hour after the bell his read was "Rocket Lab flat now, HIMS flat now. Both had huge implied moves. Option writers win again?" Per the Stocks list, Rocket Lab later sold off about 10 percent on Peter Beck calling the Neutron year-end window "narrowing," which is one word costing more than a $2.36 billion backlog earned.

Nebius goes into Wednesday carrying its own version of that risk. Per the same list, it has now admitted the roughly 300 megawatt Vineland project slips from year-end 2026 into 2027, after leadership spent weeks saying it was on track. The print is a credibility event before it is a numbers event.

4. Hitting your plan is now the thing destroying your equity value. Per Invest Like The Best, Benchmark's Eric Vishria has the cleanest frame anyone offered on software this week. The 2021 cohort of public software companies traded at 30 times revenue, has quadrupled in size, and now trades at six times. The multiple fell by a factor of six while the businesses got four times bigger.

His line to those chief executives is the part worth keeping: "you have a choice, get to AI or be worth three times revenue," and "every single day that you are hitting your plan, you are destroying equity value." The competitive frontier moved, so executing the old plan is now value-destructive rather than merely dull.

The mechanism he gives is databases, where the moat was always migration cost. Agents do not tire of translating one specification into another and the interfaces are well specified, so migration gets cheap and cost plus scaling becomes the arbiter. Behind that sits an overhang nobody is pricing: roughly 500 private software companies between $100 million and $500 million with no tender, no exit and a missed listing window.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $MU. Nine times earnings against SK Hynix at 19, with the bull case now resting on automotive and robotics rather than on price. Per the Market list, every pop above 900 has been sold for a week, and the stated rule is to avoid the upside until it closes above 900 and holds three days.
  • $HIMS. Revenue $753 million, up 38 percent against about $700 million expected, with full-year guidance raised to $3.1 to $3.3 billion, and it still round-tripped to flat because GAAP EPS was minus $0.37 against minus $0.05 and gross margin fell from 76 to 64. International went from 1.4 percent of sales to 17.4 in a year.
  • $RKLB. A record quarter, a $2.36 billion backlog up 137 percent, and a third-quarter guide well above the street, sold off on one word about the Neutron schedule. The EBITDA guide is the real soft spot.
  • $SAIL. Per Ticker Symbol: YOU, Palo Alto paid about 20 times ARR for CyberArk at announcement and 15 at close. SailPoint's $1.16 billion of ARR at those multiples implies roughly $20 billion, close to double its market cap, with non-human identities now 14 percent of managed identities and 40 percent of growth. No offer exists.
  • $INTC. Per the People to follow list, the offering was upsized to $20 billion at a $95 minimum on more than $100 billion of demand, roughly five times oversubscribed, and the stock reclaimed $100 after falling 4 percent on the announcement. Funded, dilutive and catalyst-free for about three weeks.

item.title: The memory bull just conceded the pricing lever, so I am flipping my own call
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Chip Stock Investor is holding SanDisk through a 40 percent drawdown and says the wild average selling prices are finished, locked away by five-year hyperscaler contracts.
item.content:encoded:
Chip Stock Investor is holding SanDisk through a 40 percent drawdown and says the wild average selling prices are finished, locked away by five-year hyperscaler contracts.

Yesterday I held the memory call for a third day and said I was the minority view in my own edition. Today the man still holding the stock explained why I was wrong, and he did it while defending the position.

Market context. Friday closed at a record and the internals are the argument against it. Per the Financial Markets list, S&P 500 profit margins hit 16.9 percent in the second quarter, the highest ever, the index is up 14 percent on the year after being down 7 on March 30, and the dividend yield is 1.04 percent, the lowest in history. Goldman's Panic index fell from the 90th percentile to the zero percentile in a single week. Per the Market list, Heisenberg has this on pace for one of the best Augusts in 41 years, and the only two comparables, 1986 and 2020, both gained 7 percent and were followed by Septembers that fell 10 and 8.4. Per the Market morning list, Rocket Lab and AST SpaceMobile report after the close, with Supermicro and CoreWeave tomorrow and Nebius Wednesday.

The scoreboard.

  • Reversing after fifteen days. My 60/40 that memory multiples expand before they compress is dead. I am now 55/45 the other way. Section one is the reason and it is not a sentiment change.
  • Due tomorrow. Supermicro, on Rick Orford's July 28 bearish case. It ran 31 percent into the print anyway, so this resolves on the number rather than the setup.
  • Catalyst passed, trade still live. Grab reported today and no source carries the result. The January $3.50/$4.50 call spread runs to expiry, so it stays open on its own clock.

1. The memory bull conceded the pricing lever, and that is the whole call. Per Chip Stock Investor, who is holding $SNDK through a fall from over $2,000 in July to roughly $1,200 and says nothing has fundamentally changed for the worse: "we can no longer rely on the really wild average selling prices on their SSDs. That is now over now that SanDisk and the other memory companies have signed long-term agreements, usually five-year agreements, with the hyperscalers."

Read that against what I built the call on. My 60/40 rested on Bernstein modelling roughly 35 percent of all bits shipped from 2027 to 2029 as take-or-pay at a $0.26 per gigabyte floor against $0.29 spot. I called that a floor under the price. It is the same contract structure, and from inside the position it reads as a ceiling.

Both descriptions are correct, and that is the problem. Take-or-pay at a fixed band protects the downside and removes the upside, and multiple expansion needs the upside. Nobody pays more for earnings pre-sold at a floor price for five years.

The guide says it without the framing. FY26 revenue finished up over 370 percent, the September quarter is still guided to 300 to nearly 400 percent year over year and is flat sequentially, with adjusted EPS guided to a $45 midpoint against $39.25 just reported. The answer offered is $4.5 billion of buybacks in a quarter. Companies buy back stock when the operating lever is spent.

Per the Stocks list, Jan van Eck has argued for weeks that the memory names "weren't growing volume, they just upped prices." I treated that as a bear talking his book. Today a holder said it about his own stock.

What keeps me at 55/45 rather than 70/30 is that the spot tape has not turned. Per the Market list, Bank of America has SK Hynix DRAM prices up 25 percent quarter over quarter in the third quarter, Kioxia guiding revenue up 35, and NAND spot up 5 to 6 percent on the week. Spot is still ripping. It no longer reaches the contracted book.

2. Kratos lost the competition that mattered and kept the airframe anyway. Per Rick Orford, $KTOS did $371 million of first-quarter revenue, up 23 percent, on $605 million of bookings for a 1.6 book-to-bill and a backlog near $2 billion, with full-year guidance raised. All of it posted after the Air Force passed it over in the first collaborative combat aircraft production competition, the loss that knocked the stock down.

The XQ-58A Valkyrie is flying regardless. Northrop picked the airframe for its winning US Marine Corps solution, Airbus is integrating it with a European mission system, and GE Aerospace is working on propulsion. The OpenSpace ground segment adds a Space Systems Command agreement running to a $446.8 million ceiling, and Orford is careful that a ceiling is not recognised revenue.

His bear case is fair: the Valkyrie could stay a demonstrator that never gets its own production line. The thesis is that losing the prime slot while keeping the airframe is a better business than the market priced. No target here, so size it rather than trade it.

3. CoreWeave and Nebius report into a short who has already named his price. Per Jose Najarro, who owns $CRWV six figures, June quarter consensus is $2.5 to $2.6 billion for CoreWeave and about $575 million for Nebius.

Into the prints$CRWV$NBIS
Year to date+14 percent+108 percent
Active powerover 1 gigawatt310 megawatts
Backlog or ARR$100bn backlog, 2027 ARR above $30bn, 75 percent contracted2026 ARR $7bn to $9bn
2026 capex$31bn to $35bn$20bn to $25bn, already raised
The catchinterest expense $650m to $730mmargins pre-guided lower

Najarro's single question is the right one: was the first quarter the true bottom in CoreWeave's adjusted operating margin? Management says margins expand to low double digits by the fourth quarter. If they walk that back tomorrow, the stock up 14 percent against a peer up 108 gets cheaper for a reason.

Per Edelbridge Alpha, Michael Burry is short Nebius at $211.77 and Oracle at $144.63 with Nebius near $187, and his argument is not valuation. It is that these companies depreciate GPUs too slowly, overstating Oracle's earnings by 26 to 27 percent by 2028. Two of today's sources sit thirty cents apart on Oracle. Per Stocks with Josh, he called it at $132 for a $145 minimum, hit that, and now expects continuation above $145 on an oversold RSI turn. Burry is short from $144.63 on the accounting. Only one of those has a multi-year clock.

4. Biotech is beating the tape and almost nobody is writing about it. Per the Stocks list, $XBI is up 29.5 percent this year and 10 percent on the week, the best sector print in the feed and the least discussed.

The bid is structural and dated: 33 buyouts above $500 million already this year against $200 billion to $300 billion of patent-cliff revenue pharma must replace by 2030, with three to four more deals expected in August.

Two names carry catalysts. $VERA has EFGR data next month framed as a plus 30 or minus 50 percent event. $NKTR has come back from the 50s on over $1 million of premium paid for September 100 calls, a bet on a royalty deal or a takeout inside four to six weeks.

5. Galloway put a number on the AI question and a second source answered it against the bulls. Per Prof G Markets, hyperscaler capex needs about $2.5 trillion of incremental AI revenue to earn a reasonable return, against $150 billion of cumulative AI revenue today. That is a fifteen times gap, and $2.5 trillion exceeds all of big tech's current revenue combined. The concentration underneath is sharper: OpenAI was 70 percent of Microsoft's AI sales last year and lost $21 billion.

Gavin Baker has said publicly that OpenAI is almost certainly generating significant free cash flow. Per Jordamøn, that did not survive the day. OpenAI filed a confidential S-1 on May 22, on roughly $2 billion of monthly revenue while losing $1.22 for every dollar it earns. Annualised, that is a bigger loss than the leaked figure Galloway quoted. The original listing target was September at $852 billion to $1 trillion, and SEC rules put the public prospectus about fifteen days before the roadshow, so the full financials would have had to land in late August.

I am staying 60/40 with Steve Eisman against Burry on the broad AI trade. The 40 was always customer concentration. Today it got a number rather than a new argument.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SNDK. Down about 40 percent from over $2,000 in July, still the best S&P component of the last two years, and now the clearest expression of a thesis its own bulls have narrowed. The next leg has to come from volume and buybacks rather than price.
  • $CRWV. Reports tomorrow at $2.5 to $2.6 billion consensus with a $100 billion backlog and 75 percent of a $30 billion 2027 target contracted, against $650 to $730 million of interest expense. The margin trough is the whole print.
  • $NBIS. Reports Wednesday near $187 with Burry short at $211.77 on depreciation rather than multiple. Margins were pre-guided lower, so the bear headline is scheduled and the surprise would be the capex and ARR guides going up.
  • $KTOS. A 1.6 book-to-bill, a $2 billion backlog and raised guidance, all delivered after losing the award that took the stock down. Northrop, Airbus and GE Aerospace are each building on the airframe it was passed over for.
  • $VERA. EFGR data next month framed as plus 30 or minus 50 percent, inside a sector up 29.5 percent on the year and 33 buyouts deep. Position it as the binary it is.

item.title: SpaceX printed a beat, tripled its float, and rose fifteen percent anyway
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: A 34 percent short interest that never squeezed on the print, a funding gap near $350 billion, and roughly a thousand special purpose vehicles nobody has mapped.
item.content:encoded:
A 34 percent short interest that never squeezed on the print, a funding gap near $350 billion, and roughly a thousand special purpose vehicles nobody has mapped.

This channel covered SpaceX in every edition it has published since the split. That is not because the ticker is always doing something. It is because one company ran a complete cycle in five sessions: the most crowded short in the market, a beat nobody had modelled, the largest lockup expiry of the year, and a fifteen percent rally on the day the supply arrived.

The interesting part is that the consensus was wrong at every single stage, including mine.

The week in one arc

DayWhat happened
TuesdayReports into 34 percent short interest with 95 percent of borrowable stock already lent. Consensus EPS spanned a $1.26 loss to a $0.33 profit
WednesdayBeat at $7.8 billion against $6.8 billion expected. Guided to a $100 billion exit run rate. Capex came in 39 percent hot
Thursday911.5 million shares unlock, more than 140 percent of the public float. Lowest close in company history
FridayRises 10 to 15 percent, from about $108 to $132, back above Meta's market capitalisation

Four editions, four different reasons to be wrong.

1. The print said the business is real and the balance sheet is not finished

Per the All-In Podcast, revenue was $7.8 billion, up 92 percent year over year and 67 percent sequentially, against $18 billion for all of last year. EPS came in at $0.09 against an expected 26-cent loss, with a $500 million net loss against an expected $2 billion.

Then the line that mattered more.

Q2Figure
Capex$18.4 billion in the quarter, six times a year ago, roughly a $75 billion run rate
Capex against revenue$2.35 spent for every dollar earned
2027 capex guidancenone given
Connectivity$4.3 billion revenue, $2.6 billion adjusted EBITDA
Spaceminus $200 million, call it break even
AI$2.6 billion, more than tripled sequentially

Starlink is the part that already works: 12 million subscribers, doubled year over year, at $66 a month and growing 20 percent sequentially, approaching a 24 million run rate. David Friedberg's extrapolation is $40 billion of revenue and $30 billion of free cash flow inside a year, which at 30 times would make Starlink alone a trillion-dollar company within 18 months.

The guidance is where it stops being a satellite business. Per Limitless, Elon Musk put $100 billion of annual recurring revenue by year end "if we do nothing" and pulled the $1 trillion revenue year forward from 2031 to 2030. Morgan Stanley's 2030 estimate is $325 billion. Those two numbers are not in the same universe, and the gap between them is the entire investment debate.

2. The unlock was the setup, and everyone including me had the direction backwards

Going in, the mechanics looked one-sided. S3 had 95 percent of borrowable stock out on loan and short interest at 34 percent of float. I read that as a squeeze and went 55/45 that the stock would trade higher on Thursday. It closed at its lowest price in company history instead, having shed roughly $1.6 trillion of market value since the June high.

Then Friday happened. Per the Stocks list, it ran from about $108 to $132 on the day after 911.5 million shares came free, traded 1.7 million option contracts on unlock day itself (second only to Nvidia across the whole market), and finished back above Meta's capitalisation. LuxAlgo's summary was the correct one: new rule, SpaceX unlocks are bullish.

The lesson is not that I was directionally wrong. It is that I put a date on a mechanical call. Supply cliffs are knowable in size and unknowable in timing, and a 24-hour window on a structural event is a coin flip dressed as analysis.

The supply is not finished. Per the People to follow list, the float went from 5 percent to 20 percent on Thursday and reaches roughly 40 percent by December 9, with tranches near 7 percent on August 21 and again on September 10, then smaller blocks through the autumn. Musk himself becomes eligible around 46 percent in June 2027. Tom Lee's framing is the cleanest: the company raised $18 billion in its life, is worth north of $1.4 trillion, floated $75 billion at the IPO, and over $1 trillion of stock unlocks by year end.

3. The bull case

The compute economics are genuinely better than the comparables, and that is measurable rather than rhetorical. SpaceX generates $30 million to $50 million of annualised revenue per active megawatt. CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN sit at $9.4 million to $10.4 million. Digital Realty and Equinix sit at $3.5 million to $4.4 million. SemiAnalysis puts SpaceX at roughly nine times revenue for a gigawatt of GB300 against the neocloud five-year infrastructure average.

The payback compressed. The CFO says newly deployed compute pays back inside a single calendar year, against three to four years for a typical neocloud and fifteen to twenty for real estate. A few months ago the company itself was modelling four.

Capacity is contracted and scaling. 1.4 gigawatts today, about 2 by year end, 5 to 10 next year, with line of sight to 20. At $30 million to $50 million per megawatt per year, a 6 gigawatt incremental add is worth roughly $300 billion of annual revenue on Brad Gerstner's arithmetic. SemiAnalysis models a path to $305 billion of revenue by 2027 with $235 billion, or 77 percent, from AI compute.

The sponsorship is real. JPMorgan raised its target to $240, Morgan Stanley carries $300, Argus upgraded to Buy after the quarter, Cathie Wood holds 4,051,080 shares, and Alphabet's own equity book is 95.1 percent SpaceX.

4. The bear case, and it is arithmetic rather than sentiment

The funding gap is roughly $350 billion and nobody has explained who fills it. The arithmetic comes from SouthernValue on the Stocks list.

Building 10 gigawattsFigure
Implied capex at $50 to $60 billion per gigawattabout $500 billion
Cash on hand, including the $85 billion IPO raiseabout $100 billion
Cash from operations, first half 2026$3 billion
Anthropic and Google spot GPU dealsabout $26 billion of annual recurring revenue
Estimated exit-2026 forward operating cashabout $50 billion
Residual gapabout $350 billion

The conclusion that follows is uncomfortable and it is the same structure as the OpenAI campus: Nvidia customer financing has to come into play. The chip supplier underwrites the buyer, and SpaceX has just committed to Nvidia exclusively on Vera Rubin. Gavin Baker's version is worse. At 8 gigawatts and roughly $100 billion per gigawatt, capex is $800 billion from this company alone, and component costs have already doubled in four months.

Capex is running 39 percent above expectations with no 2027 guidance. A company spending $2.35 per dollar of revenue and declining to guide the following year is asking for trust on the single largest line in the model.

The supply calendar is public and unfinished. Roughly 20 percent more of the company becomes tradable between August 21 and December 9. The Meta 2012 analogue is the honest comparable: down about 50 percent at the 91-day lockup and still down 36 percent a year later.

And there is a layer underneath that nobody has mapped. Per Diet TBPN, bankers estimate at least 1,000 special purpose vehicles hold SpaceX stock. One has already failed publicly. Late Stage Management told an investor it had sold his exposure in 2024 at roughly $105 a share, before a five-for-one split, while his portal and his 2025 tax document still showed 2,500 shares. He put in $17,250, believes the stake was worth over $300,000 at the June IPO, has filed an SEC complaint, and thinks more than 100 others are affected. Three sales executives connected to the firm pleaded guilty in February and March inside a $528 million scheme that hid markups of 10 to 100 percent and diverted roughly $88 million.

That is not a valuation risk. It is a supply risk of unknown size sitting in vehicles with no disclosure obligation, arriving into a stock whose float is already tripling.

What to do with it

Own it as a compute business, not a launch business. Connectivity and AI produce all the money. Space is break even and it is the part everyone talks about.

Let the calendar work. The tranche dates are published. There is no informational edge in front-running a supply schedule everyone can read, and Friday demonstrated that positioning into these events is more dangerous than the events themselves. The next two are August 21 and September 10.

Size for a 4-beta outcome. This is a $1.4 trillion company that has moved 30 percent in a week in both directions this month.

The single number to watch is the 2027 capex guide, whenever it arrives. That converts the $350 billion gap from an analyst estimate into a disclosed obligation, and it is the moment the vendor-financing question gets answered in public.

Watchlist for the week ahead. $SPCX into the August 21 tranche. $NBIS reports Wednesday at 105 times sales into Michael Burry's fresh short, and it is the cleanest read on whether the market still pays for neocloud growth. $MU and $SNDK, where the contracted floor held all week and the tape ignored it. $RKLB reports next week after the $8 billion Iridium deal flipped it to net debt. And $GRAB Monday and $SMCI Tuesday, both of which come due on this channel's book.

The scoreboard, Stocks & ETFs

Eight calls settled, six hits and two misses. Read the raw count with care: three of the six hits are the same SpaceX unlock catalyst carried across three editions, and two more are the same AppLovin print counted twice. Eight settled entries represent about five distinct events.

ResolvedOutcome
The August 6 unlock frees up to 911.5 million shares, Prof G MarketsHit, on the date and at the size
SpaceX at its lowest price ever with a lockup on August 6, Vest ExchangeHit
SpaceX below its $135 listing with $1.2 trillion gone, Market listHit, and it widened to $1.6 trillion
SpaceX Q2 expects $6.8 billion of revenue, Kyle ReidheadHit. Actual was $7.8 billion
AppLovin's Q2 is the first real scorecard, Milk Road, two entriesHit. Revenue grew 53 percent and the stock lost a fifth
SpaceX trades higher on Thursday, house, 55/45Miss. It fell, then rose 15 percent on Friday. Right mechanism, wrong day
Micron is the consensus dip-buy, Joseph Hogue and MarketBeatMiss. Hyperscaler memory spend went from $72.8 billion to a modelled $761 billion and $MU still had its worst month since June 2005

House record on settled calls: zero for one. One house call has resolved on this channel and it lost. There is no hit rate to quote yet and I am not going to manufacture one out of relayed calls that other people made. The honest statement is that the book is young, the only decided house position was wrong, and it was wrong on timing rather than direction.

131 open calls carried into next week. The live ones on this subject: the $350 billion funding gap, the $135 billion 2027 revenue case, the unlock schedule to 40 percent by December 9, "the unlock was the bottom", and the SPV layer. Elsewhere: the memory call at 60/40, recorded under pressure after five sessions of the complex going nowhere while the S&P made a record. AppLovin higher in three months. Eisman over Burry at 60/40. Siemens Energy rerating before the US grid names. And Damodaran's write-off tell. That is the one I most want to be watching when it triggers, because there has still not been a single major AI capex write-off and the first one will not be gentle.

item.title: Washington owns twelve public companies and just told you which ones
item.dc:creator: Kairos
item.description: Thirty government equity stakes in a year, Redwire's defence revenue up 380 percent, and the memory complex sitting 115 percent above a mean it has never failed to revert through.
item.content:encoded:
Thirty government equity stakes in a year, Redwire's defence revenue up 380 percent, and the memory complex sitting 115 percent above a mean it has never failed to revert through.

This morning's memo said to let the SpaceX calendar work. The more interesting list this weekend is the one where the government is already on the register, because twelve of those names are public and most of them have run.

The week ahead. Friday closed at the S&P's 26th record high of 2026, up over 14 percent for the year after being down 7 percent on March 30. Macro has Wednesday's CPI tonight.

The counterweight is positioning, not fundamentals. Per the Financial Markets list, Heisenberg has this on pace for one of the best Augusts in 41 years, and the only two comparables both broke: September 1986 fell 10 percent peak to trough and September 2020 fell 8.4. Per the Financial Markets morning list, Barchart has Bank of America's Bull and Bear indicator at one of the strongest stock market sell signals this century. Benjamin Cowen expects a correction to begin by late September.

The scoreboard.

  • Due Monday. Grab reports. The July 10 call was the January $3.50/$4.50 call spread with options pricing almost no move into the print.
  • Due Tuesday, and it has already run. Supermicro. Per Joseph Hogue, $SMCI is up 31 percent last week and 19 percent on the month into a print carrying a $60 billion-plus backlog, gross margin guided as high as 17 percent against roughly half that on the Street, and FY revenue near $40 billion on 80 percent growth. The criminal probe and the underwater $27.50 raise I flagged on July 28 have been swamped by the numbers.
  • Under pressure for a second day. My 60/40 that memory multiples expand before they compress. Section three is the case against me.

1. The government took stakes in thirty companies this year and twelve of them trade. Per Joseph Hogue, this is now a policy programme rather than a series of one-offs, and the terms are public.

NameThe dealMove
$MP Materials$400m preferred converting to 15 percent+145 percent since the July leak
$INTC Intel$8.9bn for 10 percent, warrants for another 5+131 percent
$USAR USA Rare Earthup to $277m direct plus a $1.3bn loan+28 percent, was as high as $26
$GFS GlobalFoundriesup to $675m across two CHIPS loans, plus 1 percentran +90, now back at the pre-announcement price
$LAC Lithium Americas$184m debt deferral, 5 percent of the company and 5 percent of Thacker Pass+11 percent
$TMQ Trilogy Metals$36m for 10 percent plus warrants for 7.5+68 percent, $68m market cap

The rest of the twelve are $LHX, $QBTS, $INFQ, $QNTM, $RGTI and $ALMU. One caution on that tail: Infleqtion trades at 57 times an expected $41 million of revenue and is the only one of the twelve net down.

The forward hook is the part nobody is trading. Washington wants domestic refining capacity back and is looking at reopening a refinery closed in 2021 that was built for Venezuelan heavy sour crude. The names under that are $VLO, the largest pure-play refiner and up 123 percent on the year, and $MPC, larger on capacity but diluted by MPLX.

This is the cleanest non-AI thesis available right now, and its edge is that the buyer has already announced itself.

2. Redwire's defence segment grew 380 percent and the market is still pricing a space company. Per Rick Orford, $RDW put up roughly $97 million to $100 million of first-quarter revenue, up about 58 percent, and the split is the story.

Redwire, Q1 2026Figure
Space segment$52.7 million
Defense Tech$44.3 million against $9.3 million a year earlier
Orders booked$186.5 million on $97 million of revenue, book-to-bill 1.92
Backlogrecord, near $500 million
Gross margin26.6 percent, up from 14.7
FY2026 guidancemaintained at $450 million to $500 million

The contracts are named: over $20 million of Marine Corps orders, a $15 million Army follow-on that is the third in eight months, and a multi-year high-eight-figure Penguin award to a NATO country. It was also selected onto the MDA SHIELD vehicle tied to Golden Dome, though that is multi-award and guarantees no revenue.

The honest gaps. Net loss was $76.5 million, over $44 million of it non-recurring including a $42.5 million Edge Autonomy stock-comp charge. Adjusted EBITDA is minus $9.2 million, free cash flow is negative, and the share count is rising to fund the transformation. No price, no multiple and no target, so this is a thesis rather than an entry.

I am 60/40 that the defence segment passes the space segment in revenue before year end. A 1.92 book-to-bill does not reverse in two quarters.

3. The memory bull case is now arguing with the chart, and the chart has history on its side. The year-to-date table is the bull case in one column. Per Evan of StockMKTNewz, fifteen S&P names have more than doubled this year and the storage and memory complex owns the top of it: $SNDK up 410.7 percent, $DELL up 260.5, $MU up 207.5, $STX up 195.1 and $WDC up 152.1.

Then per the Stocks list, the mean-reversion case. Every time the semiconductor index or $SMH has traded more than 100 percent above its 200-week average, it has reverted through the mean rather than stalling above it. Three completed instances: the index at 272 percent above in 2000, 104 percent in 2021, and $SMH at 113 percent in 2021. $SMH peaked near 180 percent above in June and still sits near 115 percent after the pullback.

The rest of the tape agrees with the chart more than with me. Korean semis fell 40 percent in 40 days. Jan van Eck's read is that the memory names "weren't growing volume, they just upped prices." FinX called the top outright. Jordi Visser has already sold Micron and rotated into silver, Bitcoin and Eli Lilly. And per the Polymarket list, Apple has started testing CXMT memory chips. That is the demand side going shopping in China for the first time.

Against all of that sits the only argument that has held: Elon Musk's line that memory supply grows about 20 percent a year against demand growing about 200. Roundhill's chief executive still calls SanDisk a $2,200 stock.

I am holding 60/40 for a third day and I am now the minority view in my own edition. What would break it is a CXMT qualification at Apple, because that converts a pricing story into a share story.

4. Visser says the crash is over and pointedly did not raise his target. Per Jordi Visser, the July drawdown was a positioning event and "the bottom is in as far as I'm concerned on a probability basis."

The confirmation is broad rather than narrow. The S&P rose 3.6 percent on the week and the Nasdaq proxy 5, with new all-time highs on the equal-weight S&P, the Russell, the NYSE Composite, the DAX and the FTSE in the same week. Earnings growth is running near 50 percent on 15 percent revenue growth, with margins at 17 percent against 13 a year ago.

His single best datapoint is on Nvidia, via Gavin Baker: it trades at its lowest forward earnings multiple in ten years, while B200 rental went from the mid $2 per GPU hour seven months ago to just under $4. Rising rental rates against a falling multiple is the shape of a market that has stopped believing the revenue.

What he did not do is raise the target. Last week he called for many AI names at new all-time highs by year end. This week he repeated the bottom call and attached no new number to it. Treat that as a call carried forward rather than reaffirmed.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SMCI. Reports Tuesday after a 31 percent week, with a $60 billion-plus backlog and gross margin guided near 17 percent against a Street at roughly half. The setup has already moved, so the risk here is the reaction rather than the number.
  • $NBIS. Reports this week. Goldman raised its 2030 revenue estimate to $35.5 billion from $22.1, a 61 percent lift, and models about $30 billion of EBITDA by 2030 on contracted power above 4 gigawatts. It rose 14 percent Friday into Michael Burry's short.
  • $SNDK. Up 410 percent this year and the cleanest expression of whichever side of section three is right. It beat on Friday and closed red, the first time the tape has ignored a good memory print.
  • $USAR. The one fully specified position on the board. Per Rick Orford, called at $13.30, near $20 now, stop raised to $18, target zone $19.75 to $21.75. He flags that his own daily signal has not crossed yet, so he is holding rather than adding.
  • $RDW. Defence revenue up 380 percent year over year with a 1.92 book-to-bill and a record $500 million backlog, still burning cash and still diluting. Own the trajectory or wait for free cash flow, but do not call it a space stock.
  • $VLO. The refining leg of the same government-capital thesis that has already repriced $MP and $INTC, up 123 percent over the past year and the largest pure-play in the group. Nobody is front-running this one yet.

item.description: Nebius reports Wednesday into Michael Burry's fresh short, Figure follows Thursday, and 745 on the tracking fund is the line that decides whether 800 is live.
item.content:encoded:
Nebius reports Wednesday into Michael Burry's fresh short, Figure follows Thursday, and 745 on the tracking fund is the line that decides whether 800 is live.

The index closed at a record on Friday and the memory complex did not move. That gap is the week in one sentence, and next week has three prints to close it.

The week ahead. Friday finished at a record high on the S&P. Per the Kalshi list, $2.8 trillion was added to the US market across the week, with the Nasdaq tracking fund up 5.3 percent. Gold still beat it, finishing almost 8 percent higher per the Stocks list, more than the two big index funds combined.

The calendar does the work from here.

Next weekWhat lands
Monday$GRAB earnings
Tuesday$SMCI
WednesdayCPI, plus $NBIS
Thursday$FIGR before the open
Also due$RKLB, $ASTS, $CRWV, $CSCO

Per Stocks with Josh, the level to hold is 745, and the path to 800 requires Wednesday's CPI to come in cool. His invalidation is unusually clean: "If at any time we cross back beneath this 745, then it means that this up move isn't likely going to happen and it means that this was the top." Set against a VIX near two-year lows and Kalshi at 67 percent for 8,000 this year, the asymmetry is not generous.

The scoreboard.

  • Due Monday. Grab reports. The July 10 call was the January $3.50/$4.50 call spread with options pricing almost no move into the print.
  • Due Tuesday. Supermicro, carrying a second criminal probe in Taiwan and a $7 billion raise whose 45 million shares at $27.50 are underwater.
  • Working. My 60/40 that the July low holds into mid-August runs to Friday, and the index closed the week at a record.
  • Under pressure, and I am saying so. My 60/40 that memory multiples expand before they compress. $MU, $SNDK, $WDC and $SKHY all went nowhere while the S&P made a new high. The thesis is contractual and the tape is not cooperating.

1. Nebius reports Wednesday into a short that just got bigger. Per Rick Orford, $NBIS has moved to a partner-funded model where partners fund, own and operate the physical build while Nebius supplies the design, the platform and the customers. The bricks are theirs, the brains are Nebius.

The guidance is the whole case: an annualised run rate of $7 billion to $9 billion by year end, from about $1.25 billion at the end of last year. Behind it sit a Meta agreement worth potentially $27 billion and 1.2 gigawatts of secured power and land in Pennsylvania. Nvidia holds a 9.3 percent stake after a $2 billion investment, and Goldman raised its own position from 7.2 to 10.5 percent this week.

The price is where it gets uncomfortable. 105.5 times sales, 7.7 times book, a 60-month beta of 4.1, and a 52-week range from about $50 to just under $300.

Michael Burry is short at $211.77 and spent this week adding to March semiconductor ETF puts and shorting more shares. This is the cleanest binary on the calendar: a 105 times sales name reporting into a famous short, with a beta of 4. I have no edge on the direction and I am not pretending to. What I would say is that a 4-beta name at that multiple is a position to size, not to be right about.

2. Mastercard grew 14 percent and the argument is entirely about the price. Per a breakdown on Reddit, revenue hit $9.28 billion, up 14 percent, with adjusted EPS of $5.04, up 21 percent, and operating margin expanding to 61.1 percent from 59.9. Expenses grew 11 percent against 14 percent revenue growth, and that gap is the EPS spread.

The mix is better than the headline. Value-added services grew 20 percent against 10 percent for the core payment network, and non-US switched volume grew 12 percent against 6 percent in the US. Cross-border volume rose 12 percent and was still running at 11 percent in July.

The poster's own conclusion is the honest one and it is not a buy: the difficulty with Mastercard is not the quality of the business, it is the valuation, and at a premium multiple even a great business produces mediocre returns if growth slows. I agree. It is still the cleanest non-AI compounder in the week's material, and the only one where the debate is price rather than durability.

3. Washington is writing cheques for minerals and lasers and almost nobody is trading it. Per the August 7 Market list, AeroVironment won a $400 million US Army contract for Locust laser defence systems, the Pentagon's first production-scale counter-drone laser award beyond prototype.

The critical minerals money landed the same week.

White House critical minerals awardsAmount
Westwater Resources, graphite$25 million
NioCorp, scandium$400 million
5E Advanced Materials, boron$8 million
HREE, magnet rare earths$4.8 million
Niron Magnetics and Standard Bauxite$150 million and $85 million

Trump announced more than $2 billion in critical mining projects plus $180 million for mining workforce education, on top of 160 mineral deals worth nearly $40 billion since January 2025.

The trade already moved once. Per Stocks with Josh, USA Rare Earth was called at $13.30 ten days ago on the magnets announcement and touched almost $20 on Friday, with the stop raised to $18 and a target zone of $19.75 to $21.75. He is holding rather than adding because the daily signal has not confirmed. Fifty percent in ten sessions earns that discipline.

4. Memory is sold out and the stocks went nowhere, and there is an arbitrage inside it. Per Milk Road AI, roughly 70 percent of hyperscaler capex is going to memory with a projected $761 billion next year, everything is sold out this year, and hyperscalers are signing three to five year contracts with price levels fixed. Elon Musk's version on the SpaceX call: memory demand is growing 200 percent a year and memory capacity is growing 20 percent.

Samsung is their pick as the laggard, with revenue up 130 percent, net profit up 52 percent, and it shipped HBM4 to Nvidia first, which retires the step-behind narrative. UBS sees it taking HBM share from SK Hynix next year.

Then the structural trade nobody will take. The NASDAQ wrapper for SK Hynix trades at a 22 percent premium, while SK Square, a holding company owning 20 percent of SK Hynix, trades at a 44 percent discount to its look-through value. Management KPIs are tied to closing that discount below 30 percent. Same asset, two listings, a 66 point spread and a paid incentive to compress it.

I am holding the memory call at 60/40 and acknowledging it has not worked for a week. Sold-out capacity with contracted pricing is a real floor. It is not a catalyst, and the tape has spent five sessions proving the difference.

Single names worth your watchlist.

  • $SPCX. Per the All-In Podcast, the first public quarter did $7.8 billion of revenue, up 92 percent, on $18.4 billion of capex in the quarter alone, roughly a $75 billion run rate. AI revenue more than tripled sequentially to $2.6 billion and Starlink's 12 million subscribers doubled year over year at $66 a month. Per the Stocks list it closed above $131, up 25 percent off the lockup, and is still 30 percent below the June listing at $1.4 trillion. The capex line is what you are underwriting.
  • $NBIS. Wednesday's print against Burry's $211.77 short, on 105.5 times sales and a 4.1 beta. Guidance says $7 to $9 billion of run-rate revenue by December from $1.25 billion. Size it like the option it is.
  • $MA. Fourteen percent revenue, 21 percent EPS, 61.1 percent margins expanding, value-added services growing double the core network. The whole question is the multiple, and nobody in the source will name it.
  • $AVAV. A $400 million Army award for the first production-scale counter-drone laser, inside a week when Washington also committed over $2 billion to critical minerals. The defence budget is the most legible non-AI spending in the market right now.
  • $PLTR. Per Chip Stock Investor, up 30 percent since the print at about $160, with US commercial revenue up 149 percent on customer count up only 35, so the growth is expansion inside accounts across 220 deals above $1 million. Their reverse discounted cash flow says $135 already implies 100 percent earnings growth for two years. Even the bulls are setting alerts below, not buying here.
  • $TLT. Macro has the driver tonight: Japan cornered, the stabilisation fund empty, the long end at an all-time low since 2002 on a 5.14 percent yield. Positioning is the whole appeal: seven puts for every call and a fifth of the float sold short, against a disclosed $82.20 cost basis targeting mean reversion to $88.
